summary: Specifies abstractly how applications and transport protocols interface with IPsec to make channels by latching connections to particular IPsec security association parameters for their lifetime.

eli5.summary: Once you pick a secret tunnel for a conversation, you stick with it. This describes the sticking.

questions: how does ipsec latching stop impersonation
what happens when an ipsec latch breaks
subtitle: Tying a connection to the exact IPsec peer and protection it started with, and alerting the application if that changes.

tldr.problem: IPsec protects packets with little regard for the upper-layer flows that use them. A changed IPsec configuration, several peers able to claim the same address, or a weak link between a peer's identity and its address can leave a live connection exposed to the wrong peer.
tldr.mechanism: Connection latching binds a connection's packet flow to the IPsec parameters in force when it started: protection type, mode, quality of protection, and local and peer identities. If a conflicting change appears, the latch breaks and the transport and application are told.
tldr.outcome: The result is an IPsec channel, layered on top of IPsec without changing its architecture. It helps guard Better Than Nothing Security (BTNS) nodes and is a prerequisite for channel binding to IPsec.

facts.label: New database
facts.value: Latch Database (LD), not kept across reboots

today: RFC 5660 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says the IPsec channel bindings and the application APIs it relies on were work in progress at the time of writing.

sections.title: The Problem: IPsec Ignores Flows
sections.content:
IPsec protects packets with little or no regard for the stateful packet flows of upper-layer protocols (ULPs). Applications relying on it for session protection are exposed to changing IPsec configurations, configurations that let several peers use the same addresses, and a weak association between peer IDs and addresses. The last can happen through wildcard matching in the Peer Authorization Database (PAD), particularly with Better Than Nothing Security (BTNS) from [RFC5386] and [RFC5387].

There are no standard APIs for applications to ask for IPsec. Applications still use hostnames and IP addresses and must rely on an IPsec configuration they may be unable to verify. This RFC lays the foundation for APIs that TCP and UDP applications can use: a way to bind the traffic flows of, for example, TCP connections to the security properties the application wants. These bindings are called connection latches, or in some contexts IPsec channels.

Latching mostly watches for updates to the Security Policy Database (SPD) and the Security Association Database (SAD) that would hurt a flow, and alerts the ULP and application before packets are sent or received under the new policy. It never changes IPsec policy databases in a way that lasts beyond the flow or a reboot, and it never changes the PAD at all.
sections.eli5: IPsec locks the mail in an armored truck but does not care which conversation each letter belongs to. Latching makes each conversation remember which truck and driver it started with.

sections.title: What an IPsec Channel Is
sections.content:
An IPsec channel is a packet flow tied to a ULP control block, such as a TCP connection, where all packets are protected by IPsec SAs such that the peer's identity and the quality of protection stay the same for the life of the flow. It is created when the flow is created, whether by a local operation such as connect() or by receiving the first packet, such as a TCP SYN. It is destroyed when the flow ends, or it is broken if the latch cannot be maintained, in which case the ULP and application are informed.

The REQUIRED latched parameters are:

  • the type of protection (confidentiality and/or integrity);
  • transport mode versus tunnel mode;
  • quality of protection (QoP): cryptographic suites, key lengths and replay protection;
  • the local identity asserted to the peer;
  • the peer's asserted and authorized identities.

The SAs that protect a channel can expire, be replaced or be re-keyed, as long as each is congruent with the latched parameters. It is desirable that channels survive the expiry of IKE SAs and child SAs. When a new SPD entry or SAD entry is not congruent with an established channel, that is a conflict.

QoP needs care because IKE initiator and responder roles are non-deterministic, so the negotiated suite is too, unless one peer offers a single suite. Implementations SHOULD offer an API to request narrow child SAs whose traffic selectors match the latch's 5-tuple, and SHOULD treat an application's request for a specific QoP as a request for narrow child SAs. If the SAs cover more than one flow, the QoP MUST be reported as indeterminate.
sections.eli5: A channel is a conversation that sticks to the same friend and the same secret code the whole time. If either changes, the conversation is marked as broken.

sections.title: Rules for Implementations
sections.content:
The RFC lists firm requirements for when a channel is desired.

  • Packets for the connection MUST NOT be sent, and inbound packets MUST NOT be accepted, until the channel is established. Early inbound packets are dropped or channel establishment fails.
  • Once established, packets MUST NOT be sent or accepted unprotected or under an SA that does not match the latched parameters. Such packets are dropped, or they terminate the channel and the application is informed before any of their data is delivered.
  • The latched parameters MUST remain unchanged once the channel is established.
  • Timeouts while creating matching child SAs MUST be treated as packet loss.
  • If the key management daemon can restart, existing latches MUST either be broken or survive the restart.
  • Dynamic IPsec policy tied to latches MUST be torn down with the latched connection and MUST NOT survive reboots.

There are also SHOULD-level items. Implementations SHOULD provide programming interfaces to inquire about, and set, latched parameters, and set values MUST be limited by system policy (the PAD and SPD) and the application's privileges. Interfaces that exist MUST expose all available peer ID information, including the peer certificate and the trust anchor it was validated to. They SHOULD expose NAT-traversal addresses and, for tunnel mode, inner and outer addresses. Implementations SHOULD create channels automatically when the application does not ask, and MAY allow that to be disabled. When IKE dead-peer detection (DPD) concludes the peer is dead or rebooted, all latches with it SHOULD be considered irremediably broken.
sections.eli5: The rules say: do not send or accept anything until the secret tunnel is ready, and once it is ready, ignore anything that does not come through that exact tunnel.

sections.title: The Connection Latch State Machine
sections.content:
A latch is always in one of four named states and always has an owner, such as a ULP transmission control block. (The text says five states but lists LISTENER, ESTABLISHED, BROKEN and CLOSED.)

  • LISTENER corresponds to the LISTEN state of TCP and other ULPs and is associated with an IP 3-tuple. It can only transition to CLOSED, and it can give rise to new ESTABLISHED latches.
  • ESTABLISHED and BROKEN represent an active latch for a flow's 5-tuple, and a latch can move between them or to CLOSED.
  • CLOSED is where a latch stays until its owner is informed.

A latch becomes BROKEN when the SAD holds SAs whose traffic selectors cover the latch's 5-tuple but whose peer or parameters conflict with it, when SPD changes would alter the protection of the latched packets, or when IKEv2 DPD concludes the peer is dead or rebooted. The owner is always informed. When all conflicts clear, the latch returns to ESTABLISHED. Most transitions are caused by the owner, and the exceptions are birth from a LISTENER, the moves to and from BROKEN, and administrative closes.
sections.eli5: A latch is either waiting for a visitor, happily connected, temporarily cut off, or finished. Trouble moves it to cut off, and fixing the trouble moves it back.

sections.title: The Normative Model: Latches in the Key Manager
sections.content:
The normative model adds a service to the IPsec key manager, the component that manages the SAD and key exchange: it manages connection latches in a new Latch Database (LD) that does not persist across reboots. The abstract interface the ULP uses has five calls, and one call goes the other way.

Creating a connection latch succeeds only if no conflict exists in the SPD and SAD. If the parameters are not given and no suitable SA exists, the key manager MUST initiate child SAs, and if needed an IKE SA, to derive them. The key manager MAY delay child SA setup and return after the policy check, which may require a fleeting LARVAL state the RFC does not describe further.

The key manager MUST prevent conflicts among latches and between a latch and existing or proposed child SAs. A child SA conflicts with a latch if its traffic selectors match and its peer, type of protection or QoP differ. Proposals that conflict SHOULD be narrowed (see Section 2.9 of IKEv2, RFC 4306). If that is not possible, the key manager MUST break the latch and inform the holder before accepting the conflicting SAs. For SPD changes that would weaken or bypass a latched flow, the REQUIRED behavior is to move conflicting latches to BROKEN. An OPTIONAL behavior is to logically add a PROTECT entry matching only that 5-tuple, which MUST NOT survive crashes or reboots.

When a latch breaks, the ULP MUST stop sending and MUST drop incoming packets for the connection until it returns to ESTABLISHED, and connection-oriented ULPs SHOULD act as though the connection is losing packets. On an administrative close, connection-oriented ULPs MUST act as though the peer reset the connection.

The RFC works through an example in which hosts A and B talk TCP on port 4000 under a policy that protects TCP ports 1-5000 with ESP for peers holding credentials from CA X. If a third host C tries to impersonate B to A after A's latch exists, C's SAs break the latch and the TCP connection is reset. If A does not support latching, C can impersonate B to A, though without seeing the cleartext it is limited by TCP sequence numbers to attacks such as RST attacks.
sections.eli5: A helper at the front desk keeps a list of who is on each call. If someone new pretends to be your friend, the helper tells you right away and you hang up.

sections.title: Other Models and Optional Features
sections.content:
An informative second model uses local packet tagging. The ULPs keep latch state, and the IPsec layer tags inbound packets with the SAD index of the SA that protected them, while outbound tags carry the latched parameters or ask for feedback about the SA used. These tags never appear on the wire. This model has no explicit BROKEN state, can cache part of the SPD in the ULP, and extends naturally to connectionless datagram use. It may not work with ESP/AH offload hardware that cannot do such tagging.

A third, informative model covers non-native IPsec such as bump-in-the-stack and security gateways. They have no APIs at the endpoints and must infer connection state from packet inspection, and may have to fake a reset by sending TCP RST packets. This model is not suitable for channel binding.

Optional features make latching more active. With optional protection, an application could ask for protection where policy would bypass, or privileged applications could ask to bypass where policy would protect. Local policy must permit it, and the SPD MUST then be logically updated atomically at latch creation to match the exact 5-tuple, without surviving crashes or reboots. Latching also supports simultaneous TCP connects when both sides request the same parameters; if they request different ones, the latch must fail on one or both ends.
sections.eli5: There are other ways to build the same idea, such as sticking little name tags on every packet, and some ways need extra permissions. The first way is the official one.

sections.title: Latching for TCP, UDP and SCTP
sections.content:
For TCP, a listener creates a LISTENER latch, a SYN received for a listener or sent by the host creates an ESTABLISHED or BROKEN latch, and any move of the TCP connection to CLOSED closes the latch. For UDP, latching works with simulated connections, such as connected sockets, or with datagram-tagging APIs.

SCTP is different because each endpoint can have several IP addresses but only one port. The RFC represents this as multiple 5-tuples, each with its own latch, giving N x M latches for an association where one end has N addresses and the other M. Implementers may instead extend the latch to hold several addresses. Latches are created or closed as ASCONF chunks add or delete addresses.

For TCP and SCTP a BROKEN latch can be handled by (a) waiting for it to recover, (b) acting as if a reset or ABORT arrived, or (c) acting as if an ICMP destination unreachable arrived, which triggers path failover in multi-homed SCTP. Implementations MUST provide a default and SHOULD let applications be informed or choose. The RFC recommends (b) when only one path remains and (c) for multi-homed SCTP, reasoning that a conflicting SA most likely means the original peer is gone and failing faster seems reasonable. It argues this does not create off-path reset attacks, because the attacker must first establish a conflicting SA with an endpoint.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of connections use the same idea. When a latch breaks, the quickest sensible thing is usually to hang up, unless there is a backup path to switch to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In its minimal form, latching is a passive, local feature layered on IPsec: transports are notified of conflicts, notified when they clear, must drop inbound packets and must not send for affected connections. It needs a new database, the LD, which may mean significant changes inside some IPsec implementations, but it does not modify the basic IPsec architecture.

Latching is not negotiated, so one end may latch while the other does not. Policy changes at the non-latched end can then send packets unprotected. The latched end rejects them, but sensitive data may already be exposed, so applications SHOULD check that both ends are latched. Latching does not guarantee that two connections between the same addresses have the same peer IDs; such applications can compare the latched parameters themselves. It protects against TCP RST attacks, but not if the original peer is no longer reachable.

Without IPsec APIs, latching gives only marginal benefit over plain IPsec. Latches can be broken by on-path attackers, and by off-path ones who can attack routers or cause an endpoint to accept an ICMP Redirect, so latching does not protect specifically against on-path denial of service. The RFC considers it acceptable to break latches when DPD concludes a peer is dead. Optional features can have non-local effects by preventing distributed policy changes from taking full effect, so administrators SHOULD be able to break ESTABLISHED latches.
sections.eli5: Both friends need to use the trick for it to work fully. It stops strangers from sneaking in, but it cannot stop someone who is standing on the path and simply cuts the string.

items.desc: Returns a latch handle or an error.
